interest: This document is exceptionally valuable to historians of U.S.-Japanese relations during the 1930s as it illuminates the escalating mutual suspicion, security anxieties, and intelligence friction preceding the Pacific War through the lens of port courtesies and vessel clearance. It reveals how the informal reciprocal agreements of 1930–1931 permitting visits on local notification broke down by late 1935 under pressure from the U.S. Navy Department, which demanded strict diplomatic prior notification to monitor Japanese naval tankers suspected of conducting covert surveillance of strategic Pacific locations including Hawaii, Midway, and Wake Islands. Furthermore, the file demonstrates the extensive inter-agency coordination between the State Department, Navy, War Department, Customs, and Immigration authorities, capturing the sharp contrast between ceremonial goodwill tours by Japanese midshipmen and deepening military tensions.
overview: This file comprises the Department of State's official List of Papers (docket register sheets, Form DS-46 and continuation sheets) for Decimal File 894.3311, titled 'Visits of Vessels and Aircraft of Japan to Ports of the United States,' encompassing sub-numbers 143 through 289 from January 1930 to May 1936. The register records communications and purports of correspondence exchanged between the Department of State, the Japanese Embassy in Washington, the Navy Department, the War Department, the Treasury Department (Customs), the Labor Department (Immigration), and various state and municipal authorities. Major subjects include the negotiation, operation, and eventual termination at the end of 1935 of informal reciprocal arrangements permitting entry of unarmed public vessels upon local notification to ports of the United States and the Philippines versus American vessels to Japanese ports; tensions arising from unannounced schedule changes, early arrivals, and refusals to supply officer rosters by Japanese naval tankers (such as the Erimo, Sunosaki, Sata, and Tsurumi); intelligence monitoring of Japanese vessel activities near Midway and Wake Islands; and extensive arrangements for official goodwill cruises by the Japanese Navy's Training Squadron (cruisers Iwate and Yakumo) and mercantile training ships (Taisei Maru, Hakuyo Maru, Kaio Maru, and Nippon Maru).

subfiles.about: Official Department of State List of Papers and docket purports recording correspondence and actions regarding visits of Japanese naval, auxiliary, and training vessels to United States and Philippine ports between 1930 and 1936.
subfiles.summary: This 26-page docket register (Form DS-46 and continuation sheets) details official correspondence and purports of communications filed under decimal number 894.3311 from January 1930 to May 1936. It documents the evolution of U.S. and Japanese policy governing visits of unarmed public vessels and warships to respective ports, tracing the operation of the 1930–1931 informal reciprocal agreements and their termination on December 31, 1935, in favor of strict prior notification through diplomatic channels. Significant attention is given to the movements of Japanese naval oil tankers (such as the Sunosaki, Sata, Tsurumi, and Erimo), quarantine enforcement, pilotage fees, unannounced schedule shifts, and military intelligence observations of Japanese activities at Midway and Wake Islands. In addition, the file chronicles diplomatic arrangements, port courtesies, itinerary coordination, and presidential audiences for successive goodwill training cruises by the Japanese Training Squadron (cruisers Iwate and Yakumo) and mercantile training vessels (Taisei Maru, Hakuyo Maru, Kaio Maru, and Nippon Maru).
